analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill, introduced in August 2012 with no cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died without ever getting a vote when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes on transferring very large amounts of wealth between generations. Repeal would apply to anyone dying or giving assets away after the bill became law. The bill had a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, went only to committee, and never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and recipients of the largest fortunes. The estate tax generally only applies to estates above a high dollar threshold, so eliminating it delivers its biggest dollar benefit to the wealthiest families, and repealing the gift tax lets wealthy people pass money to relatives tax-free during their lifetimes. Estate-planning lawyers and advisors who earn fees managing wealth transfers would lose work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire portion of the tax code covering estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, so no estate or large lifetime gift would owe federal transfer tax after enactment [S3].

Because the estate tax only reaches the largest estates, the largest inheritances would receive the largest tax savings; smaller estates, already under the filing threshold, would see little or no change [S3].
The repeal takes effect immediately for deaths, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers occurring after the date of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, who would have to make up the lost federal revenue through borrowing, other taxes, or lower spending. The estate tax is a revenue source that falls almost entirely on very large inheritances, so its repeal shifts the tax burden away from that group.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes eliminates an entire category of federal taxation on the transfer of great wealth, adding to the deficit unless the revenue is replaced elsewhere [S3].

The benefit is concentrated: estates small enough to escape the tax already gain nothing, so the repeal functions as a tax cut aimed at the largest family fortunes rather than a broad tax relief measure [S3].

Supporters of repeal argue the tax can force heirs of family farms and small businesses to sell assets to pay the bill; the bill does not address that concern narrowly, but instead ends the tax for all estates of every size, including the very largest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow — heirs of the biggest estates keep millions they would otherwise owe — while the cost is diffuse: the federal government loses a tax paid almost exclusively by very large inheritances, so everyone else's share of funding the government rises. A narrower fix aimed only at farms and small family businesses could have addressed the stated concern without ending the tax on the largest fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Griffin of Arkansas introduced the bill on August 2, 2012, near the end of the 112th Congress [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No cosponsors signed on, no committee action followed the referral, and no vote was ever held; the bill died with the end of the Congress on January 3, 2013 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers overall are no worse off, since the estate, gift, and transfer taxes remained on the books and continued to apply to the largest estates. The bill's intended beneficiaries — heirs of very large fortunes — gained nothing, because no vote ever occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; the estate tax stayed

for.name: Rep. Tim Griffin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate and gift tax repeal bill on August 2, 2012 and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 2, 2012 and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill was introduced by a single Republican with zero cosponsors, so there was no measurable split on the floor.

industries.note: Had it passed, repeal would have eliminated the tax owed on the largest inheritances and lifetime gifts, a benefit that grows with the size of the fortune. The lost revenue would be spread across all other taxpayers.

A thriving practice area — structuring estates and gifts to minimize transfer taxes — would largely disappear if the taxes were repealed. In this case the industry's interest in keeping the tax happens to run alongside the public's interest in the revenue.
